lesson.title: Sorting Frequencies: What a Filter Actually Does
lesson.summary: A filter is a circuit whose output depends on the frequency of its input, built to pass some frequencies through largely unchanged, the passband, while suppressing others, the stopband.
lesson.body:
Every filter is built around one core fact from Frequency Response: the impedance of a capacitor, 1/(ωC), shrinks as frequency rises, while the impedance of an inductor, ωL, grows as frequency rises. Resistors, by contrast, do not care about frequency at all. By combining resistors with capacitors and or inductors, you can build a circuit whose output to input ratio, its transfer function H(jω) = Vout/Vin, changes shape depending on frequency, favoring some frequencies and discriminating against others. That deliberate frequency-dependent shaping is what makes a circuit a filter rather than just an amplifier or a plain divider.

The frequencies that a filter lets through with little or no attenuation form the passband, and the frequencies it suppresses form the stopband, terms introduced in Passband and Stopband. Between them lies a transition region where the response falls off gradually rather than switching instantly, because real filters cannot have infinitely sharp edges. Exactly where the passband ends and the stopband begins is a design choice, conventionally marked at the point where output power drops to half its passband value.

Because filter responses can range from full passage down to attenuation by a factor of a thousand or more, engineers describe attenuation on a logarithmic scale, the decibel: dB = 20 log10(|H|), where |H| is the magnitude of the transfer function. Suppose a filter's output amplitude in the stopband is one tenth of its input amplitude, so |H| = 0.1. Then the attenuation is 20 log10(0.1) = 20 times (minus 1), which is minus 20 dB. That figure, 20 dB for a factor-of-ten drop in amplitude, will come back repeatedly once you study how fast filters roll off between passband and stopband.

Depending on which frequencies fall in the passband and which fall in the stopband, filters are sorted into families: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-reject, and the special case of the notch filter. Each family solves a different practical problem, and each is built from the same basic ingredients, resistors, capacitors, and sometimes inductors, arranged in different topologies. The chapters ahead walk through each family in turn.
